extracted.intended_audience: artists, architects, art historians, and students of art/architecture (readers of Ruskin-style criticism)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and critical principles for judging Gothic architecture and related visual art, and for distinguishing Purist, Naturalist, and Sensualist tendencies in painting and sculpture. Emphasises truthfulness, subject-selection, ornament, vegetation, rigidity, and moral purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist stance: Purist vs Naturalist vs Sensualist
rubrics_metrics.description: Three classes of artists — Purists, Naturalists, Sensualists — defined by what they select from nature: the Purist 'receives from nature and from God that which is good for him', the Sensualist 'fills himself with the husks that the swine did eat', and the Naturalist 'takes all home' and represents the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tripartite classification to diagnose an artist's aesthetic: Purists select and idealize; Naturalists strive to represent whole nature (both good and bad); Sensualists delight in vice or the merely exciting. Beware conflating Naturalists with Sensualists: Naturalism aims at comprehensive truth, not at indulgence in evil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalism (represent the whole of nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Naturalist 'takes the human being in its wholeness, in its mortal as well as its spiritual strength' and represents 'the whole range of its passions' fearlessly, making the subject noble in all its acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works on breadth of sympathy and courage to portray varied states (haste, anger, sensuality, pride, fortitude, faith). Naturalism should bring 'one majestic harmony' out of diverse elements rather than exploit them for mere shock or sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purism (selection of what is absolutely good)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Purist aims to represent what is 'absolutely good for some special purpose or time', effacing transitory passions and favoring chastened, often emaciated or ascetic types over strong, passionate life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess Purist works for restraint, moral elevation, and deliberate selection. Watch for over‑Purism: choosing the least or the falsely highest good (shortsighted or weak judgment) that brings discredit to selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensualism (delight in vice, decay, or excitements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensualists habitually contemplate humanity in poverty, decrepitude, fury or sensuality and prefer subjects of decay, disorder, and disease or vice portrayed 'without any moral purpose'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag anti‑patterns where scenes of suffering, vice, or filth are presented for excitement or 'to quicken the dull spirit' (e.g., gratuitous torture, sexualized nymphs, or revels). Such choices can stimulate temporary excitement but produce moral and artistic impoverishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral purpose and subject selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Art should not portray vice or misery 'for the sake merely of the excitement' and true choice of act/pose should promote charity or insight rather than disgust; selection of the act is critical (Murillo's beggar-boys vs alternatives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge subject selection by its likely ethical and imaginative effect: does it invite sympathy, reform, or understanding, or merely gloat over degradation? Examples: showing hunger with wistfulness vs showing mere disgusting mannerisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and scale of truth (surface fact vs inner truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: A love of veracity is prized, but beware 'seizes on a surface truth instead of an inner one' — imitation of superficial appearance may miss symbolic or spiritual meaning (purgatorial fire example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise inner, symbolic, or conceptual truth over mere imitation of surface detail. When truthful detail is used, it must serve deeper meaning; otherwise it is 'want of thought' or vanity in selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of design and fact (unity of invention and truthfulness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic builders 'belong to the central rank' that unite design with fact: they received principles of design but added a love of fact and truthfulness that the South lacked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a work successfully integrates disciplined design with faithful representation of factual detail. Warning: excessive devotion to fact can despise design; excessive purism can ignore fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veracity in portraiture and humility in representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic art practices truthful portraiture: it does not exalt kings into demi-gods nor saints into archangels, but gives full kingliness or sanctity 'mixed with due record of their faults'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess portraiture for honest recording of virtues and faults, and inclusion of common life in backgrounds; consider whether the work leaves judgment to the viewer, like Scripture history, rather than manipulating sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of everyday life and domestic customs
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic sculpture and painting 'fill up the backgrounds' with 'the most familiar scenes and most simple subjects' and are 'copious records of all the domestic customs and inferior arts' of their age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value works that incorporate ordinary life and material culture as meaningful context or symbol. Such inclusion strengthens historical veracity and communal relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fondness for vegetation and accurate rendering of plant forms
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'peculiar fondness for the forms of Vegetation' distinguishes Gothic work; the living foliage became a subject of intense affection and accurate study, not merely an accessory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use detailed observation and accurate depiction of leaves, tendrils, and flowers as evidence of a Gothic temper: signals gentler, rural, and thoughtful life. Excessive transgression of material/design laws in pursuit of vegetal accuracy is a possible pitfall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rudeness and changefulness as humility and energy
rubrics_metrics.description: Rudeness (confession of imperfection) and a love of change are elements of Gothic spirit: confession of the workman's imperfection and the subject's imperfection manifests humility and vitality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish wholesome rudeness (honest craftsmanship, communal labor) from crude incompetence. Rudeness can be virtuous when coupled with charity and depth of feeling; evaluate intent and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active rigidity (rigidity as energetic tension)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Rigidit y' is defined as active rigidity: energy that gives tension to movement and stiffness to resistance (e.g., Gothic vaults and traceries show elastic tension, ornament 'prickly independence').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess Gothic work for lines of force, angular tension, and structural expression that convey energy rather than passive mass. Rigidity should express strength and resolve; beware excess that becomes perversity of purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal expression of ornament — prominence and nervosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic ornament 'stands out in prickly independence' — crockets, pinnacles, thorny frets, and nervy entanglements rather than languid flow; ornament expresses energy and framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge ornament by its articulation of structural energy and independence. Excessive brusquerie may betray overindulgence; insufficient energy may indicate Southern/languid temper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes and cultural sources of stylistic traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Features like rigidity stem from habits: hard rapid working, cold climate, delight in cold, strength of will and independence of character found in Northern peoples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualize stylistic attributes historically and culturally: material, climate, labour practices, and moral habits shape aesthetic choices. Use social-historical causes to explain, not excuse, artistic excesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redundance (ornamental accumulation) as humility and social function
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Redundance' — the uncalculating bestowal of ornament — is characteristic and partly humble: richness addresses both the rudest and the most refined minds and is a form of communal sacrifice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate accumulation of ornament as both aesthetic and social: it can be virtuous humility and popular appeal, but should be judged against taste for restraint. Some best Gothic works balance redundancy with simple loveliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for balance among Gothic elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The Gothic spirit comprises several elements (rudeness, changefulness, naturalism, rigidity, redundancy) and the best architecture unites them; 'the best Gothic building is not that which is _most_ Gothic'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overall judgement should weigh elements against one another. Excess in any single impulse (especially rigidity) can corrupt the style; prefer balanced syntheses over maximalist expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti‑pattern — delighting in foulness or gratuitous detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Depicting filth or degradation 'as if no human imagination were vigorous enough for its conception' (e.g., exposing dust on a beggar's sole) is 'mere delight in foulness' rather than truthful art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark down works that exhibit voyeuristic attention to degrading details for their own sake. Truthful depiction must aim at understanding or moral consequence, not exhibitions of grime.
